# 1 Chronicles 4:23–43 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Passage

This section closes the genealogies of Judah (v. 23) and then turns to the tribe of Simeon (vv. 24–43). The Simeon material falls into three parts: (a) the clan genealogy and its relative smallness (vv. 24–27); (b) the list of cities and villages occupied until David’s reign (vv. 28–33); and (c) the military expeditions of Simeonite chieftains during Hezekiah’s time into Gedor and Mount Seir (vv. 34–43).

---

## v. 23 — The King’s Potters

**Traditional Reading**

- **Ellicott** explains that “Netaim” means “plantations” (cf. Isaiah 17:10) and “Gederah” is a town in the Judean Shephelah (Joshua 15:36). The phrase “with the king in his work they dwelt there” indicates that these pottery works were a royal establishment — much like the royal porcelain works at Sèvres in France. The linen-weavers of Beth-Ashbea (v. 21) may also have been included in this royal service. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Gill** notes two possible interpretations: either these were literal potters and gardeners/hedge-makers working for the king of Judah, or — less likely — that after the Babylonian exile some chose to remain doing menial work for the Babylonian king. He also notes that “Netaim” and “Gederah” may be proper place-names in Judah. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Clarke** records that the Targum interprets these “potters” spiritually as “disciples of the law, for whose sake the world was created.” But Clarke himself sees them more practically as brickmakers and potters who lived in low grounds and dug clay for the king’s building projects. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

**Homiletical / Devotional Readings**

- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** preached a famous sermon titled *“With the King for His Work!”* (No. 1400, 1877), drawing four points: (1) Our King has many kinds of servants — soldiers, watchmen, heralds, scribes, musicians, potters, and gardeners; none should despise another. (2) All who live with the King must work — “They did not live on the king’s bounty … to do nothing, but they dwelt there *for his work*.” (3) Those who work for the King ought to live *with* Him — close communion with Christ is the secret of effective service. (4) We are working *for the King* — this dignifies the humblest task. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_1chronicles]

- **Alexander Maclaren (Baptist)**, in *“The King’s Potters,”* emphasises that (a) Christians “dwell with the King” by faith even while living among the “plantations and hedges” of this life; (b) dwelling with the King must precede doing His work — communion fuels service; and (c) the King’s work is far broader than conventional “church work” — it covers all common duties done for Christ’s sake. He adds that the potters’ work “went to Jerusalem … It was for the king. What can be too good for him?” [https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/1-chronicles/kings-potters.cfm]

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic leaning)** summarises Spurgeon’s four points and adds: since the broad focus of these chapters is the tribe of Judah and David’s line, these men receive special mention because they “worked for the king and lived with the king.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/]

---

## v. 24 — The Sons of Simeon

- **Ellicott** notes that the Pentateuch has three lists of Simeon’s sons (Genesis 46:10; Exodus 6:15; Numbers 26:12). Genesis and Exodus name six sons; Numbers and Chronicles name five, omitting Ohad. “Jarib” here is “Jachin” in Numbers. Genesis and Exodus read “Jemuel” for “Nemuel” and “Zohar” for “Zerah.” Exodus 6:15 notes that Shaul was “son of a Canaanitess,” and his mixed-race clan was the only one that became populous (see vv. 25–27). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Clarke** observes that the genealogy here differs from Genesis 46:10 and Numbers 26:12, likely because the same person bore multiple names. He concludes: “to reconcile is impossible; to attempt it, useless.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran)** adds that Simeon’s descendants were “classed together with those of Judah, because they had their possessions within the boundaries of Judah.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## vv. 25–27 — Shaul’s Line; Simeon’s Small Numbers

- **Ellicott**: “His brethren had not many children” refers to the other Simeonite clans (cf. Numbers 26:12), not Shimei’s literal brothers. The contrast is with the children of Judah, who multiplied greatly. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Clarke** supplies the census data: at the first wilderness census Simeon numbered 59,300 (Numbers 1:23); by the second census they had plummeted to 22,200 (Numbers 26:14) — a loss of 37,100, making them the smallest tribe. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran)** comments that this lack of multiplication “in those days was looked upon as a special visitation of the Lord” and ties it to Jacob’s curse in Genesis 49:7, where Simeon and Levi are told they will be scattered in Israel. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Guzik / Enduring Word**: The census data confirms the population collapse during the wilderness period. He also quotes John Trapp: “Of this tribe was that shameless fornicator, Zimri (Numbers 25), as also Judas Iscariot, as Jerome affirmeth.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/]

- **Garner-Howes (Baptist)**: “They were never a strong tribe, seeming to be dominated by Judah among whom they dwelled.” No prominent persons from Simeon are mentioned in Israel’s history. The tribe’s ultimate destiny is “one of the enigmas of the Scriptures.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## vv. 28–31 — Simeonite Cities Until David’s Reign

- **Ellicott** heads this section “The Seats of the Simeonites until the Reign of David.” The cities listed (Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, etc.) are all in the arid southwestern portion of Judah. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran)** explains that David, “because the Simeonites had been too cowardly to drive the heathen from some of the towns allotted to them, took these cities from the hands of their enemies and gave them to his own tribe of Judah.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Clarke** adds that Ziklag in particular was taken by David (1 Samuel 27:6). Because the Simeonites withdrew allegiance from David’s house, the kings of Judah extended their domination into Simeonite territory, forcing the Simeonites to seek new pasture at Gedor and Seir (vv. 39–43). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Guzik** notes that Simeon and Levi were cursed to be scattered after the Shechem massacre (Genesis 34; 49:5–7), so Simeon never had its own province — only these cities and villages within Judah’s territory. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/]

---

## vv. 32–33 — Villages and Genealogical Record

- **Ellicott**: “And their genealogy” — literally, “and they had their own registration (or enrolment).” Though their settlements lay within Judah’s territory, their clans were registered as belonging to a distinct tribe. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann**: The five villages (Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, Ashan) and their surrounding settlements “unto Baal” were their habitations, and “according to these cities they were entered into their genealogical lists.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## vv. 34–37 — The Thirteen Princes of Simeon

- **Ellicott** calls these “the thirteen princes (emirs) of Simeon who headed the expedition of their tribe in the age of Hezekiah (fl. 710 B.C.).” None of them are otherwise known. He notes that “Jaakobah” is literally “to Jacob” — a patronymic like the English surname “Jacobs.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann** counts thirteen leaders and heads of families: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah, Joel, Jehu, Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, and Ziza. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 38 — Increase of the Clans

- **Ellicott**: “These mentioned by their names” is literally “these who have come (forward) with names” — i.e., have been adduced by name. “Were princes in their families” = *ameers* or chieftains in their clans. Their father-houses “had spread greatly,” which prompted the search for new territory. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann**: The families “increased greatly, in numbers and strength,” leading to the first expedition. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 39 — The Journey to Gedor

- **Ellicott**: “Gedor” here can hardly be the Judean hill-country town of Joshua 15:58. The Septuagint (LXX) reads **Gerar** (Γεραρα). The “valley” whose east side they reached is likely the Arabah, below the Dead Sea — a location consistent with the later move to Mount Seir and the Amalekites. The search for pasture “proves that even so late as the reign of Hezekiah, those Israelite clans which bordered on the desert were still nomads, like the Bedouins.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann**: This was “a first expedition or migration” to “the entrance of Gedor, or Gederah, a district noted for its fertility.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 40 — Rich Pasture and the Hamites

- **Ellicott**: “Fat pasture and good” — if Gerar is the correct reading, compare Genesis 26:17ff (Isaac’s experience there). “The land was wide” is literally “broad of both hands” — an open plain. “Quiet and peaceable” echoes the description of Laish in Judges 18:7. “They of Ham” = Hamites or Canaanites (cf. 1 Chronicles 1:8). “Of old” = *lephânîm*, “before” — i.e., before the Simeonite invasion. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Clarke**: These Hamites were “probably either Philistines or Egyptians, who dwelt at Gedor, which was situated in the environs of Joppa and Samnia.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann**: “They of Ham” were “probably a tribe of the Canaanitish branch of the children of Ham.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 41 — The Attack in Hezekiah’s Days

- **Ellicott**: “These who were written by name” are the emirs of vv. 34–37. The Hebrew text reads “the wells,” but the margin reads “the Maonites” (a very similar Hebrew word). The LXX reads τοὺς Μιναίους (the Maonites or Minæans). The Maonites appear to have been sojourners from Maon, south of the Dead Sea near Petra (modern Ma‘ān; cf. 2 Chronicles 20:1). “Destroyed them utterly” = devoted them to God for destruction (ḥērem, as in Joshua 6:17). Ellicott adds that this practice was “not peculiar to Israel, but was common to the Semitic races,” citing the Moabite Stone where King Mesha devoted 7,000 inhabitants of Nebo to ‘Ashtar-Chemosh. “Unto this day” refers to the time when the original source was written, long before the Chronicler compiled it. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Gill**: The expedition came in Hezekiah’s later fifteen years (after the Syrian army was destroyed), following Dr. Lightfoot’s calculation. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Kretzmann**: Both Hamites and Meunites dwelling together were exterminated, and the Simeonites “occupied their land until the exile.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 42 — The Expedition to Mount Seir

- **Ellicott**: “Went” could be translated “had gone (marched).” The time is not stated, but the wording strongly suggests this expedition was contemporaneous with the Gedor campaign. “Of them” (the 500 men) refers back to the clans that had already struck the Hamites. Neither Ishi nor his four sons (Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, Uzziel) are otherwise known. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann**: This was “a second expedition” — 500 men went to Mount Seir in Edom. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Gill** notes a rabbinic tradition (recorded by Kimchi) that the four captains were from the tribe of Manasseh, not Simeon (cf. 1 Chronicles 5:24), but Gill rejects this: since the 500 were “of the sons of Simeon,” the captains were surely of the same tribe. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 43 — The Amalekite Remnant Destroyed

- **Ellicott**: “The rest of the Amalekites that were escaped” is literally “the remnant of the survivors (pelêtâh) belonging to Amalek.” These were Amalekites who had taken refuge in Seir from Saul’s and David’s exterminating wars (1 Samuel 14:48; 15:7; 2 Samuel 8:12). He also notes that 1 Chronicles 1:36 presents Amalek as a partly Edomite stock. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran)**: This final destruction of the Amalekites fulfilled God’s threatened judgement in 1 Samuel 15:3. The Simeonites “dwelt there unto this day” — meaning they remained there until the time of the Chronicler. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Gill**: The Amalekites who escaped Saul’s sword — though Jewish tradition says 100,000 were slain by Saul in one day — and David’s sword (though 1 Samuel 27:8 says David left “neither man nor woman alive”) were finally destroyed by these Simeonites. The phrase “unto this day” refers to the time of Ezra, the presumed author of Chronicles. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-chronicles-4.html]

- **Clarke**, citing Calmet, places this expedition around the time of the captivity of the ten tribes, when the Simeonite remnant felt compelled to retire southward into Arabia Petraea. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

---

## Denominational Perspectives

### Baptist
- **Spurgeon** (v. 23): Stresses that all believers are servants of the King and must work, not coast. He connects the potters and gardeners specifically to Sunday-school teachers: potters mould clay while it is soft (children’s hearts); gardeners tend plants within the enclosure (the church). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_1chronicles]
- **Maclaren**: Emphasises personal communion with Christ as the indispensable prerequisite for all Christian work. “Dwelling with the King must go before doing His work.” [https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/1-chronicles/kings-potters.cfm]
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: Treats Simeon’s scattered destiny as “one of the great enigmas of Scripture” and draws the lesson that “even most persons of great prestige and position are forgotten with time.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-chronicles-4.html]

### Lutheran (LCMS)
- **Kretzmann**: Emphasises (a) the cowardice of Simeon in not driving out the Canaanites from their allotted cities — David had to do it for them; (b) the fulfilment of Jacob’s curse; (c) the extermination of the Amalekites as the long-delayed fulfilment of God’s explicit command in 1 Samuel 15:3, showing that “the wrath of God finally did exterminate the Amalekites, as He had threatened.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-4.html]

### Methodist / Wesleyan
- **Adam Clarke**: Takes a characteristically practical and devotional approach. He emphasises the sincerity of Jabez’s prayer earlier in the chapter with an extended moral application (“Reader, imitate the conduct of this worthy Israelite”). On v. 23, he notes the Targum’s spiritualised reading (potters as “disciples of the law”) but prefers the literal interpretation. On the Simeonite expeditions, he supplies geographical and historical context (citing Calmet). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_chronicles/4.htm]

### Reformed / Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)**: Draws the link between Simeon’s scattering and the prophecy of Genesis 49:7. Notes that Simeon’s land was “only within the arid southwestern portions of Judah” (citing Payne). He also highlights Spurgeon’s devotional reading of v. 23 at length. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/]

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
- **Ellicott** (representing the best of 19th-century critical scholarship) notes text-critical details throughout: the LXX reading “Gerar” for “Gedor” in v. 39; the Hebrew margin reading “Maonites” for “habitations” in v. 41; the Moabite Stone parallel for ḥērem warfare. He also stresses that “unto this day” in v. 41 refers to the time of the *original source*, not the Chronicler’s own time. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/4.htm]

- **Payne** (cited by Guzik): Notes that Simeon’s territory was limited to “arid southwestern portions of Judah” and that elements of Simeon either moved north after the kingdom divided or adopted northern religious practices (cf. Amos 5:5, condemning Beersheba along with Ephraim’s shrines). Other Simeonites “carried on in a seminomadic life in isolated areas.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/]

- **NET Bible** notes and **Bible Odyssey** articles were not available in the searches conducted.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
- No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this passage was retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org in the available searches.

### Prosperity / Word of Faith Teaching
- The prayer of Jabez (earlier in the chapter, vv. 9–10) has been heavily used in prosperity-gospel and Word-of-Faith circles (notably Bruce Wilkinson’s *The Prayer of Jabez*), but the specific verses 23–43 were not flagged in the sources searched as being central to that debate. The passage was not found discussed from a prosperity perspective in the available sources.

---

## Summary of Key Themes

1. **Royal service dignifies humble work** (v. 23): Potters and gardeners — ordinary trades — are recorded in Scripture because they worked “with the king for his work.” This is the dominant devotional takeaway across traditions.

2. **Simeon’s decline fulfils prophecy** (vv. 24–27): Jacob’s curse of scattering (Genesis 49:7) worked out in history through population decline, lack of independent territory, and eventual absorption into Judah.

3. **God’s purposes advance even through obscure people** (vv. 34–43): The thirteen named Simeonite chieftains are unknown elsewhere, yet under Hezekiah’s reign they expanded Israelite territory, executed divine judgement on the Hamites and Meunites, and finally destroyed the Amalekite remnant — fulfilling the long-delayed command of 1 Samuel 15.

4. **Pastoral nomadism persisted late** (vv. 39–40): Even in the 8th century BC, Israelite border clans remained semi-nomadic, seeking pasture like the patriarchs.
